advantage.what_would_change_it: a third party verifying both the outputs and the resource counts (the prepared state is now decided by Stim as well, but the gate counts, depth and clocks are still this package's accounting), the comparison repeated on hardware connectivities with each tool's own router, and a sampling referee at wide widths that decides the whole outcome distribution rather than a family of projections (the wide block now decides exact marginals at 32 qubits, so the full distribution is still only decided at 12). The shared corpus, the Stim sampling task and the marginal referee are three of those conditions, not all of them
advantage.why: the GHZ and ring rows compare a construction grammar that knows those targets against a synthesizer that is general over stabilizer states, and the random-state row is the case where the grammar has nothing to say. A cheaper circuit for a target the grammar was written for is a measurement about that target, not a general advantage, and no claim of general superiority is made here. On the shared corpus, where no construction is specialised, the two-qubit counts agree on every one of 75 matched instances and the grammar's only measured saving is depth -- median 3.25x, quartiles 2.75-3.75, range 1.50-5.00 across the sample -- which is a schedule difference a rescheduling pass can also produce, and the routed corpus is the measurement of that: with each engine's own router on a recorded device the two land within a few percent of each other at the median and Qiskit is the shallower of the two on more instances than not

equivalence.task: decide whether two circuits compute the same operation, on a corpus constructed so the two referees disagree

limitations: One host, one Qiskit version, one run per row: the wall clocks are single measurements, not medians, and they are here to show the scale of the synthesis cost rather than to be quoted as a ratio.

Qiskit's synthesizer is general over stabilizer states and this package's grammar is not. The GHZ and ring rows are the favourable case for the grammar by construction, which is why the random-state row exists.

Three random stabilizer states at three widths are three samples, not a distribution over stabilizer states; they exist to show that the grammar's abstention is structural rather than a property of one state.

The line topology task still routes Qiskit's circuit with THIS package's router. The device routing task and the routed corpus are the counterparts: Qiskit is given a recorded device coupling map and its own transpiler, and this package's router runs on the same device graph. One seed and one optimisation level are recorded because SABRE is stochastic; each routed instance is one router run, not a median over seeds.

The routed corpus compares each engine as shipped, which is not the same optimisation problem on both sides: Qiskit's transpiler searches an initial layout, routes and keeps its final layout, while this package starts from the identity placement, routes with its lookahead router and restores logical qubits to their original wires. The comparable number is the pre-restore routed depth; the total is reported beside it. A router-only difference -- a layout search this package does not do -- is therefore part of what the routed rows measure, and it is not priced.

Qiskit keeps its final layout rather than restoring it, so its routed circuit is decided against the target relabelled by that layout. This package restores logical qubits to their original wires; both its pre-restore depth (the comparable routed number) and its total depth (the cost of fixed-wire verifiability) are reported rather than one number being chosen to flatter either engine.

The device routing rows price a SWAP as one two-qubit gate on both sides. No CNOT-equivalent restatement is made in this task; that accounting belongs to the placement record, where its arithmetic is checked.
Gate counts and depth are not fidelity, latency or error rate. There is no device calibration, error model or classical-control cost anywhere in this record.

MQT QCEC is compared on the equivalence task only, and on one corpus: pairs whose relation is fixed by the construction that built them, of which seven are one angle apart on a tolerance ladder. It decides the standalone unitary question, so its verdicts are compared with this package's standalone verdict and never with the controlled or prepared-state ones -- a scope difference is recorded as a scope difference. Near its own numerical threshold its verdict changed between identical runs, so the record carries a distribution of criteria there instead of a verdict, and the threshold is reported as measured rather than as the value its configuration declares. It is given no timeout, its own default tolerance, and one corpus: it has not been run on synthesis, on routing, on sampling, or on any workload of this repository's own.

The Stim comparison is sampling only, and its referee is exact arithmetic in two shapes: the full outcome distribution at 12 qubits, and the exact marginal on chosen wire subsets above that (16, 24 and 32 qubits). A marginal is a projection, not the distribution -- two different states can share every tested marginal, and every graph state is uniform in the Z basis, so no Z-basis marginal separates one graph state from another. The wide rows say 'these projections are right', not 'the state is right', and the uniform-marginal target is in the block so that limit is measured rather than asserted. It says nothing about Stim's ceiling: the throughput ratio compares a Python per-shot tableau clone with Stim's compiled C++ sampler, and Stim's published 20,000-qubit surface-code workload is not addressed by any row here. No memory measurement was taken on either side.
The two engines drew independent seeds, so the pair comparison is two independent samples of one state rather than paired trajectories.

Peak memory is resident-set growth measured in a child interpreter per engine, with the peak counter reset after the engine's imports and the specification's rebuild, so it is the sampling step's own growth and not the ~165 MiB floor numpy and this package's imports cost before a shot is drawn. It is resident memory, not bytes allocated: an engine that recycles heap it already touched shows less than one that allocates fresh, and that is a property of the allocator as much as of the engine. It is one run per engine rather than a median, it measures no GPU and no allocator-internal bookkeeping, both engines' outcome tables are inside the window, and it is not a ceiling claim about Stim -- no 20,000-qubit workload is measured here.

The shared corpus is a sample from this package's own generators: five widths, five independent draws per cell, three graph families, plus one random stabilizer state at each of three widths. That fixes the weakness of a hand-picked set -- every family is reported as a distribution -- but it is not graph space. The widths are five tiers, the draws come from one pairing-model generator and one tree-plus-edges generator, and instances at the same width share that width; no claim about the distribution of all graph states is made.

The bootstrap intervals in the corpus summary resample the instances in this sample. They describe how much another draw from the same seeded generator could have moved a median, and are not confidence statements about graph space. The per-instance quartiles and ranges are reported beside them so the width of the distribution is visible without them.

On the graph states both engines emit one entangler per edge, so the two-qubit counts agree by construction; the corpus measures schedule and abstention, not a gate-count advantage. The depth gap is a layering difference and a transpiler scheduling pass could close it, which is why it is recorded as a schedule result and not as synthesis superiority.

Both engines' outputs are now decided twice: by this package's specification referee and by a third party -- Stim's tableau simulator, an independent implementation (`apedp_dyn.vqc.foreign_referee`). That second opinion covers the prepared state and nothing else: gate counts, depth and wall clock are still this package's accounting, and the bridge from this package's IR to Stim's circuit is ours, so a translation bug shared by both referees would not be caught. It is also Clifford-only -- a non-Clifford circuit is `REFUSED` rather than verified, which is an abstention and not a loss.

tools.note: same input as this package: signed Pauli stabilizer strings. Qiskit's synthesiser is general over stabilizer states; the local construction grammar is not, which is why the random-state row matters as much as the GHZ rows. Its transpiler is also used for the routing task, on a recorded device coupling map, because routing Qiskit's circuit with this package's router would measure this package's router

tools.note: wired for execution, not synthesis: each engine receives the same signed stabilizer strings, samples the same number of shots, and both sample sets are decided against the exact distribution. The workload is 12-qubit wide because the referee enumerates the distribution exactly; the throughput ratio is an implementation comparison (Python per-shot tableau clone against Stim's compiled C++ sampler), not a ceiling for either engine, and Stim's published 20,000-qubit workload is not addressed
tools.task: Z-basis sampling from a stabilizer specification, on the same targets, the same shot budget and the same seeds policy

tools.note: wired on the pairs where a comparison can say something. QCEC decides with decision diagrams, ZX rewriting and simulation-based falsification, and is given its own default numerical tolerance rather than one tuned to agree with this package. It decides the standalone unitary question only: it has no controlled or state-preparation mode, and near its threshold identical calls can return different criteria, which the record reports as a distribution instead of a verdict
tools.task: circuit equivalence checking on a corpus built so the two referees disagree, with every divergence attributed to a threshold, a scope or an abstention

verdict.abstentions: all three tools ran on the task each of them overlaps with, so there is no unavailable-tool abstention left to report; what remains are per-pair abstentions inside the equivalence task, where a tool that declined is recorded as declining rather than as losing. No claim of state-of-the-art performance rests on the large-width rows recorded elsewhere, and none of these tools was run on synthesis, sampling and equivalence alike: Qiskit on synthesis and routing, Stim on sampling, QCEC on equivalence
verdict.asymmetry: on a random stabilizer state this package abstains and Qiskit synthesizes; that row is recorded because a comparison that only ran the favourable case would not be a comparison
verdict.corpus_routing: on 75 corpus instances routed onto fake_sherbrooke (127 qubits, 144 edges) with each engine's own router -- Qiskit's transpiler with its own layout search and no restore, this package's lookahead router with the restore ladder reported separately -- Qiskit's routed circuit is shallower on 53% of instances, median depth ratio 0.97x [quartiles 0.88-1.10] with its own spread by family: random_graph 1.05x [0.96-1.11], regular3 0.88x [0.82-0.98], regular4 1.00x [0.91-1.06]. The abstract depth gap does not survive routing: the two routers land within 3% of each other at the median, Qiskit is shallower on 40 of 75 instances and this package on 31 -- partly because Qiskit's transpiler searches an initial layout while this package starts from the identity placement on a sparse device graph
verdict.device_routing: on 4 logical circuits routed onto fake_sherbrooke (127 qubits, 144 edges), Qiskit's own transpiler wins 2 of 4 routed-depth comparisons against the lookahead router (median ratio 1.47x) and 2 of 4 against greedy (median 1.32x). Which engine is shallower depends on the circuit: Qiskit wins on ghz balanced_tree, qiskit synth ghz, this package on ghz chain, ring 100. Both routers and both routed and total depths are reported rather than the number that would flatter one engine
verdict.equivalence: on 18 pairs whose relation is fixed by the construction that built them, the two referees agree on 11 and differ on 2 where a threshold decides, while on a further 2 the other tool has no single answer: repeated identical calls returned equivalent and equivalent_up_to_global_phase and no_information. Both apply a threshold and neither is the arbiter: this package decides at 1e-09 on the per-amplitude Frobenius distance and QCEC at a numerical tolerance of its own (2.27e-13, as its configuration declares it), which are not the same quantity; the corpus fixes the exact answer on every ladder pair and both distances are recorded beside the verdicts. 2 pair(s) above the dense bound are decided by QCEC and refused here (an abstention on this side), 0 are declined by QCEC, and 1 prepares one state from two different unitaries, where QCEC answers the unitary question and this package's own unitary verdict agrees with it. No divergence is left unexplained.
verdict.sampling: on 3 of 3 12-qubit targets both samplers are CONSISTENT with the exact distribution and the two sample sets AGREE on 3 of 3; median throughput 4,737 vs 5,449,452 samples/s. That ratio is implementation, not ceiling: Python tableau clones against a compiled C++ sampler
verdict.sampling_memory: resident growth during the sampling step, measured in a child interpreter whose peak counter is reset after its imports: at 12 qubits the median is 1.0 MiB for this package and 3.0 MiB for Stim, and above the enumerable width 1.5 against 3.4 MiB, over an import floor of 167 and 171 MiB that is charged to neither engine. The number that moves is the outcome table, not the width: a 32-qubit GHZ keeps two outcomes and grows 0.3 MiB here, while a 32-qubit random state with 20,000 distinct outcomes grows 8.7 MiB on both engines -- which is why the gap between the two samplers is a few megabytes of implementation and not an order of magnitude, and why neither number is a ceiling claim: Stim's 20,000-qubit workload is not measured here
verdict.shared_corpus: on 75 of 78 sampled targets both engines prepare the state; the grammar abstains on the 3 random stabilizer states. Two-qubit counts agree on every matched instance, so there is no gate-count advantage to report. Depth is reported as a spread over the sample, not as one row: median ratio 3.25x (qiskit/grammar), quartiles 2.75-3.75, range 1.50-5.00; the grammar is shallower on 75 of 75 instances. Per family the median depth ratio is random_graph 2.65x, regular3 3.50x, regular4 4.00x. That is a schedule difference, not a gate-count one, and the spread is the size of the effect a single instance would have misreported
verdict.synthesis: on a 100-qubit GHZ the grammar uses 99 two-qubit gates against 4950 (x50), depth 12 against 395; on a 100-qubit ring state it uses 100 two-qubit gates against 100 (x1), depth 101 against 199. Both sides are decided VALID against the same specification by the same referee, so the difference is in the circuits, not in the verdict
verdict.target_dependence: the two-qubit-gate advantage is target-specific: large on GHZ, absent on the ring state, where a general Gaussian-elimination synthesizer reaches the same two-qubit count as the hand-written construction
verdict.third_party: both engines' circuits are decided twice: by this package's specification referee and by Stim's tableau simulator (1.16.0), which shares no code with it. On 75 matched corpus instances and 75 routed ones the two referees agree on every circuit -- 300 decisions, all VALID, no disagreement recorded -- so adjudication is not self-referential. Stim decides the prepared state, not the gate counts, and the bridge from this package's IR to Stim's circuit is ours; both limits are in the limitations
verdict.wide_sampling: above the enumerable width the referee is the exact marginal on 190 wire subsets, up to 32 qubits: 190 of 190 of this package's marginals pass the Bonferroni-corrected chi-square and 190 of 190 of Stim's, with 0 disagreeing subsets between the two engines and 102 subsets whose exact marginal is uniform (the graph-state blind spot, recorded rather than avoided). Median throughput 1,797 vs 6,757,430 samples/s, the same implementation gap as at 12 qubits

wide_sampling.subset_design: every adjacent pair of wires plus three 10-wire projections (contiguous, strided, seeded draw) of each target; each subset's exact distribution is derived from the specification by Gaussian elimination over GF(2), so the referee is arithmetic rather than either sampler
wide_sampling.task: sample Z-basis outcomes above the width where the full distribution is enumerable, decided by exact marginals of the specification
wide_sampling.two_sample_null: two independent correct samplers at the same shot count on the same subset, so the pair is only reported as DISAGREE beyond sampling noise
wide_sampling.what_it_does_not_decide: a projection, not the distribution: a state that differs from the target only on wires no tested subset covers passes, which is why the tested subsets are listed in every row, and every graph state is uniform in the Z basis, so no marginal of this kind separates one graph state from another -- the ring_graph row is in the block to show that (all of its marginals are uniform) rather than to claim a verdict it cannot support
